title: Minimal Polynomial Reduction and Annihilator Theory
description: Proves that any polynomial function of a matrix can be reduced modulo the minimal polynomial: aeval M f = aeval M (f mod minpoly K M). Shows the minimal polynomial generates the annihilator ideal and gives the sharpest degree bound. Compares minpoly vs charpoly reduction: minpoly is at least as tight. Proves the nonderogatory characterization: minpoly = charpoly iff charpoly generates the annihilator ideal. 30 theorems, 0 definitions, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The minimal polynomial appears in Frobenius's 1879 work on the rational canonical form, where he showed that the cyclic decomposition of K^n as a K[X]-module is governed by invariant factors d₁|d₂|...|d_k with d_k = minpoly. Sylvester (1851) and Hermite (1854) studied matrix polynomial identities earlier, but the systematic treatment of the annihilator ideal came with Emmy Noether's module theory (1921) and the general PID structure theorem. The annihilator ideal Ann(M) = (minpoly K M) is a simple consequence of K[X] being a PID: ideals are principal, and the minimal generator of Ann(M) is the monic minimal polynomial. Leopold Kronecker recognized the practical importance of minimal polynomial reduction for matrix computation. In modern applications: the Cayley-Hamilton reduction (using charpoly) was long standard, but minimal polynomial reduction is strictly better for derogatory matrices — scalar matrices like cI have minpoly = X-c of degree 1, enabling trivial polynomial reduction vs degree-n charpoly reduction. The Lean 4 file proves the complete theory: reduction theorem, degree bounds, annihilator ideal, power reduction, and a catalog of special cases (scalar, nilpotent, idempotent, involutory).
overview.problemStatement: Prove that the minimal polynomial gives optimal polynomial reduction for matrix evaluation: $f(M) = (f \bmod \mu_M)(M)$ with $\deg(f \bmod \mu_M) < \deg(\mu_M) \leq n$. Show $\{p : p(M) = 0\} = (\mu_M)$ as a principal ideal. Prove the nonderogatory characterization: $\mu_M = \chi_M \iff$ the annihilator is generated by $\chi_M$.
overview.text: For any polynomial f and n×n matrix M, aeval M f depends only on f mod minpoly(M). This is the optimal reduction: the remainder has degree < deg(minpoly) ≤ n. The ideal {p : aeval M p = 0} is principal, generated by minpoly(M). A matrix is nonderogatory (minpoly = charpoly) iff this ideal is generated by charpoly. This characterization connects to control theory: M is nonderogatory iff the associated linear system is observable/controllable.
overview.proofStrategy: Use Mathlib's Polynomial.modByMonic_add_div (division algorithm) and minpoly.aeval for the zero property. Prove minpoly annihilates M. The annihilator ideal = (minpoly) uses minpoly.dvd (forward: any annihilating polynomial is divisible by minpoly). Special cases (nilpotent, idempotent, involutory) follow the pattern: show the specific polynomial annihilates M, then apply minpoly.dvd. The full file covers 10 sections with 30 theorems from basic reduction through special matrix classes.
keyInsights: The polynomial evaluation map f ↦ f(M) factors through K[X]/(μ_M): two polynomials give the same matrix function iff they're congruent mod minpoly — the matrix algebra K[M] is isomorphic to the quotient ring K[X]/(μ_M)

The annihilator ideal Ann(M) is principal because K[X] is a PID — the unique monic generator is minpoly, making it the algebraic invariant that completely determines all polynomial relations satisfied by M

The degree hierarchy deg(r) < deg(μ_M) ≤ deg(χ_M) = n has two potentially strict inequalities: the gap deg(χ_M) - deg(μ_M) measures 'derogatory-ness', and scalar matrices cI achieve maximum gap (1 vs n)

Matrix powers M^k are spanned by {I, M, ..., M^{d-1}} where d = deg(minpoly): this is K[M] as a finite-dimensional K-algebra, and the coefficients come from reducing X^k modulo minpoly via the division algorithm

The special matrix catalog (nilpotent: μ = X^d, idempotent: μ | X(X-1), involutory: μ | X²-1) shows how the minimal polynomial encodes the spectral type: nilpotency index, eigenvalue set, and Jordan block structure
Every proof follows the same template: (1) find an annihilating polynomial q, (2) invoke minpoly.dvd to get μ_M | q, (3) use the degree/factorization of q to constrain μ_M
prerequisites: Polynomial arithmetic: remainder, division, degree bounds
Module theory: annihilator ideal, principal ideal domains

conclusion.summary: A comprehensive 447-line, 30-theorem formalization of minimal polynomial reduction theory. All results are machine-verified with 0 sorries. The file spans: core reduction (f(M) = (f mod μ_M)(M)), degree bound hierarchy, the annihilator ideal = (μ_M), power reduction (M^k via minpoly basis), comparison with charpoly reduction, and a catalog of special cases (scalar, identity, zero, nilpotent, idempotent, involutory). The file demonstrates systematic application of a single algebraic principle — the division algorithm — across many matrix contexts.
conclusion.implications: The minimal polynomial reduction formula `aeval M f = aeval M (f %ₘ minpoly K M)` is the gateway to several deeper results: (1) the rational canonical form decomposition of K^n as a K[X]-module, where the cyclic summands are annihilated by the invariant factors; (2) matrix function computation via minpoly (e^{tM} is a polynomial in M of degree < d = deg(minpoly), reducing 2^k matrix multiplications to d multiplications); (3) observability and controllability in linear control theory (Kalman's conditions reduce to minpoly = charpoly); (4) the Cayley-Hamilton theorem becomes a special case of the annihilator ideal theory. The idempotent and nilpotent cases connect to spectral decompositions: any diagonalizable matrix decomposes as a sum of idempotents, and any nilpotent is a sum of nilpotent rank-1 matrices.
openQuestions: Formalize the rational canonical form: K^n ≅ K[X]/(d₁) ⊕ ... ⊕ K[X]/(d_k) with d₁|...|d_k, where d_k = μ_M
Prove that μ_M = lcm(μ_{M,v₁}, ..., μ_{M,vₙ}) for any basis v₁,...,vₙ, where μ_{M,v} is the annihilator polynomial of v
Formalize matrix exponential via minpoly reduction: e^{tM} = ∑_{k=0}^{d-1} p_k(t) M^k for explicit polynomials p_k
Extend to primary decomposition: μ_M = ∏ pᵢ^{eᵢ} (distinct irreducibles) and the corresponding K^n = ⊕ ker(pᵢ^{eᵢ}(M))?

sections.title: Module Documentation and Mathematical Overview
sections.summary: Header comment establishing the file's role in the Cayley-Hamilton hierarchy, listing 5 key results, and documenting applications (matrix functions, control theory, Jordan form). Variables: field K, Fintype n, DecidableEq n.

sections.title: Part 1: Minimal Polynomial Reduction Theorem
sections.summary: Core theorem: aeval_eq_aeval_mod_minpoly (f(M) = (f mod μ_M)(M)) via division algorithm and minpoly.aeval. Companion: aeval_sub_mod_minpoly_eq_zero (f - f mod μ_M is annihilated).

sections.title: Part 2: Degree Bounds from Minimal Polynomial
sections.summary: Two degree bounds: degree_mod_minpoly_lt (reduced degree < deg(μ)) and degree_mod_minpoly_le_dim (reduced degree < n). Uses calc chain: deg(r) < deg(μ) ≤ deg(χ) = n.

sections.title: Part 3: Annihilator Ideal = (minpoly)
sections.summary: Ideal closure lemmas (add, mul_left, mul_right). Core iff: annihilator_iff_minpoly_dvd (aeval M f = 0 ↔ μ_M ∣ f). Corollary: charpoly_multiple_of_minpoly (μ_M ∣ χ_M).

sections.title: Part 4: Congruence Modulo Minpoly
sections.summary: Two iff theorems: congruence_mod_minpoly (same remainder → same evaluation) and aeval_eq_iff_minpoly_dvd_sub (equal evaluations ↔ minpoly divides difference).

sections.title: Part 5: Matrix Power Reduction
sections.summary: power_eq_aeval_mod_minpoly (M^k = aeval M (X^k mod μ_M)) and aeval_reduced_by_minpoly (every evaluation = one of degree < deg(μ) or zero). K[M] spanned by {I,...,M^{d-1}}.

sections.title: Part 6: Minpoly vs Charpoly Reduction Comparison
sections.summary: Three degree lemmas: minpoly_degree_le_charpoly, minpoly_degree_le_dim, minpoly_degree_pos. Key: charpoly_mod_refines_to_minpoly shows charpoly reduction further reduces to minpoly reduction.

sections.title: Part 7: Special Cases — Scalar, Identity, Zero Matrices
Part 8: Nilpotent Matrices — Minpoly = X^d
sections.summary: nilpotent_from_minpoly: μ = X^d → M^d = 0 (via minpoly.aeval + map_pow). nilpotent_higher_powers: M^d = 0 → M^k = 0 for k ≥ d (via pow_add + zero_mul).

sections.title: Part 9: Polynomial Identities via Annihilator Theory
sections.summary: aeval_eq_of_minpoly_dvd_diff (explicit witness form of congruence), minpoly_multiple_annihilates (multiples of μ annihilate), annihilating_degree_ge_minpoly (any nonzero annihilator has degree ≥ deg(μ)).

sections.title: Part 10: Idempotent and Involutory Matrices
sections.summary: Idempotent M² = M: annihilated by X²-X, so μ | X(X-1) (eigenvalues 0 or 1, M is a projection). Involutory M² = I: annihilated by X²-1, so μ | (X-1)(X+1) (eigenvalues ±1, M is a reflection).
